p: Four men named James appear in the New Testament. The church has long read this one as the Lord's brother.
b: Iakobos is the Greek form of Jacob, one of the most common Jewish names. The New Testament knows James son of Zebedee, whom King Herod had killed (Acts 12:1-2); James son of Alphaeus; James the father of Judas (Luke 6:16); and James the brother of Jesus (Matthew 13:55; Galatians 1:19). The writer needs no title beyond his name, so he was someone every church knew. That fits James the Lord's brother, the leader of the Jerusalem church (Acts 12:17; 15:13; 21:18), whom Josephus says the high priest Ananus had stoned (Antiquities book 20, quoted by Eusebius). Whether he wrote the letter himself is discussed on the opening pages.
r: Acts 12:2; Acts 12:17; Acts 15:13; Acts 21:18; Galatians 1:19; Galatians 2:9; 1 Corinthians 15:7; Matthew 13:55; Jude 1:1

a: a slave of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ
p: James calls himself a slave of God and of Jesus, and never mentions being Jesus' brother.
b: Doulos is the ordinary word for a slave, and this site keeps "slave" (as at Jude 1:1, "a slave of Jesus Christ"). Many English Bibles soften it to "servant". In the Old Testament "slave of the LORD" was an honor given to Moses, David and the prophets, so the word is both humble and proud. James puts "God" and "the Lord Jesus Christ" side by side as the one master he serves. If he is the brother of Jesus, his silence about that tie is striking; Jude does the same, calling himself only "a brother of James".

a: the twelve tribes in the Dispersion
t: The twelve tribes in the Dispersion
p: Jews scattered outside the land, Jewish believers in Jesus among them, or the whole church as God's Israel?
b: "The Dispersion" (diaspora, as in John 7:35) was the Jewish name for Jews living outside the land of Israel, from Babylon to Rome. Readers take the address three ways. (1) Jewish believers in Jesus living abroad, written to by the leader of the mother church in Jerusalem, as Acts 15:23 sends a letter from Jerusalem to believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. (2) The whole church, Jewish and Gentile, seen as the restored twelve tribes living as exiles in the world, as 1 Peter 1:1 seems to use "Dispersion". (3) All the scattered Jewish people, to whom James writes as a Jewish teacher. The letter's Jewish world (the synagogue of 2:2, the law, Abraham, Rahab, Elijah) suits the first reading best, though it does not exclude the second.

t: The same greeting as the Jerusalem letter
p: Only two other New Testament letters open with plain "greetings": the Jerusalem letter of Acts 15 and a Roman officer's letter.
b: Chairein, literally "rejoice", was the everyday opening of a Greek letter. Paul never uses it; he writes "grace and peace". In the New Testament it opens only three letters: this one, the letter that James and the Jerusalem elders sent to the Gentile believers (Acts 15:23, "greetings"), and the commander Claudius Lysias' letter to Felix (Acts 23:26). It is a small link with Acts 15, where James speaks. James also plays on the word at once: chairein (greetings) is followed by charan (joy) in the next verse.

t: "Brothers" and the women of the church
p: James' adelphoi takes in the whole church, women as well as men.
b: James calls his readers "brothers" fifteen times. The Greek masculine plural was the normal word for a mixed group, and James shows he means women too when he speaks of "a brother or a sister" in need (2:15). This site keeps "brothers" in the Plain English Translation, as Acts, Romans and the other letters do, with the gloss "brothers and sisters". The word belongs to Jewish speech ("your brothers", Deuteronomy 15:7) and makes the letter sound like a family talk.

t: Trial and temptation are one Greek word
p: Peirasmos means both a hardship that tests you and an inner pull toward sin. James uses both senses here.
b: In 1:2 and 1:12 peirasmos means a trial from outside: poverty, unfair treatment by the rich (2:6), sickness (5:14). In 1:13-14 the verb peirazo means being tempted to do wrong. English needs two words, so the Plain English Translation says "trial" and "tempt", but James is making one argument: the same hard moment can prove faith (1:3) or become a pull toward sin (1:14), and God sends no one the second (1:13). The Lord's Prayer has the same word: "do not bring us into testing" (Matthew 6:13).

p: James, Paul and 1 Peter all link joy, trouble and endurance, perhaps from a shared early teaching.
b: Jesus told his followers to be glad when they are insulted and persecuted (Matthew 5:11-12). Paul writes: "We know that trouble builds endurance" (Romans 5:3), and 1 Peter 1:6-7 also speaks of joy while faith is tested like gold. The three passages share words (testing, endurance, joy), which may point to a pattern of teaching the early church passed on. Joy here is not a feeling about pain but a way of counting it, since hardship is producing something (1:3-4).

p: Teleios runs through James: complete endurance, a complete gift, the complete law, the complete man.
b: Teleios means having reached its goal: grown up, finished, whole. Older English Bibles say "perfect", which can sound like "flawless". This site uses "complete" in James every time the word appears (1:4, 1:17, 1:25, 3:2) so the reader can see that James keeps returning to it: God's gifts are complete, his law is complete, and the believer is meant to become complete. Jesus' "So you are to be perfect, the way your heavenly Father is perfect" (Matthew 5:48) uses the same word. A second catchword follows: "short of nothing" (1:4) leads into "short of wisdom" (1:5), the same Greek verb leipo.

p: Haplos means simply, without strings or second thoughts, and so generously.
b: The adverb haplos comes from a word for "single" or "undivided". God gives with a single mind, and that is the point of the next verses: the one who asks must not be "double-minded" (1:8). God gives without scolding (me oneidizontos), unlike the patron who reminds you of every favor. The promise echoes Jesus: "Keep asking, and it will be given to you" (Matthew 7:7). Jewish wisdom also taught that wisdom is God's gift to those who ask (1 Kings 3:9-12; Proverbs 2:6).

p: The verb diakrinomai means to be divided against yourself. James uses it again for a church that divides people (2:4).
b: Diakrinomai can mean to doubt, to argue or to make distinctions. Here it is a person split down the middle, trusting God and not trusting him. James returns to the word in 2:4: a church that seats the rich man in front has "drawn lines" (diekrithete). A divided heart and a divided church go together. Wisdom from above, by contrast, is adiakritos, "unwavering" (3:17).

p: Dipsychos means "two-souled", a person with two wills pulling two ways.
b: James uses the word here and in 4:8. It matches a Hebrew idea: the psalmist accuses liars of speaking "with a divided heart" (Psalm 12:2), literally "a heart and a heart". Israel's great command asks for the opposite: "Love the LORD your God with all your heart" (Deuteronomy 6:5). In James the double-minded man prays and doubts (1:6-8), blesses God and curses people (3:9-10), wants to be a friend of God and of the world (4:4, 8).

t: Is the rich man a brother?
p: James does not say whether "the rich one" belongs to the church. The answer changes the tone of the verse.
b: The Greek sentence gives the lowly man the word "brother" but leaves the rich man without it. (1) Many read him as a rich believer: let him boast in being humbled, because his wealth counts for nothing before God. (2) Others read the verse as irony about a rich outsider: his only "boast" will be his fall, since he will wither like grass. James' other words about the rich (2:6-7; 5:1-6) are all aimed at people outside the church, which supports the second reading. The first fits the verb "boast", which the sentence shares with the lowly brother. Either way the old order is turned over, as in Mary's song: "He has pulled rulers down from thrones and raised the lowly high" (Luke 1:52).

a: like a wildflower he will pass away
p: James borrows Isaiah 40's picture of grass and flowers, as 1 Peter 1:24 also does.
b: Isaiah 40:6-7 says: "All flesh is grass, and all its loyal love is like a wildflower. The grass dries up, the flower wilts." James applies the picture to the rich in particular. In the land of Israel the wildflowers of spring can vanish in a day when the hot dry wind blows off the desert (see the next note). Isaiah goes on: "but our God's word will stand forever" (Isaiah 40:8), and James soon speaks of the word that saves (1:18, 21).

p: Kauson can mean burning heat or the hot east wind off the desert.
b: In the Greek of Jonah 4:8 the "hot east wind" that God sends against Jonah is pneuma kausonos, a wind of kauson. Coming with the sunrise here, it may be that wind rather than the sun's heat alone. People in the land of Israel knew how fast it could turn green slopes brown. The picture fits a writer who knew that country.

p: James speaks like the Psalms and like Jesus' beatitudes.
b: "Blessed is the man who..." is a Jewish form of praise for a way of life, like Psalm 1:1 ("Happy is the person who does not walk by the advice of the wicked") and Jesus' beatitudes (Matthew 5:3-11). This site renders the Hebrew ashrei "Happy" in the Psalms; the Greek makarios in the New Testament is "Blessed". James has another beatitude in 1:25 and calls the enduring "blessed" in 5:11.

p: The winner's wreath of the games, given here for endurance.
b: A stephanos was a wreath of leaves or gold given to winners at the games and to honored citizens, not a king's crown. "The crown of life" means the crown that is life itself, eternal life. Revelation 2:10 promises the same thing: "Stay faithful all the way to death, and I will give you the crown of life." The promise is for "those who love him", the language of the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:5) and of 2:5.
orig: τὸν στέφανον τῆς ζωῆς (ton stephanon tes zoes)

a: It is God who is tempting me
t: "Do not say, 'The Lord made me fall'"
p: James answers an excuse that Jewish wisdom had already rejected.
b: Sirach, a Jewish wisdom book of the 100s BC (part of the Bible for Catholic and Orthodox Christians), says: "Do not say, 'It was because of the Lord that I fell away,' for you will not do what he hates. Do not say, 'He led me astray'" (Sirach 15:11-12). James makes the same point. There is a tension with Genesis 22:1, "God put Abraham to the test", where the same Greek verb is used. James' answer is that God tests faith so that it grows (1:3), but he never pushes anyone toward evil. Evil cannot tempt God, and God does not tempt anyone with it.

p: James locates temptation in human desire, much as Jewish teaching spoke of the yetzer hara, the inclination to evil.
b: Genesis says that "what the human heart shapes is evil from youth on" (Genesis 8:21; compare Genesis 6:5). The Hebrew word for what the heart shapes, yetzer, became the rabbis' name for the evil inclination in every person. Sirach 15:14 says God made humankind and "left him in the hand of his own inclination". James' wording is close to this way of thinking: temptation comes from within, from desire. The verbs are from fishing and hunting: desire "drags off" (exelko) and "baits" (deleazo) its prey.

p: Desire conceives, sin is born, and sin grows up to bear death. In 1:18 God gives birth to a different family.
b: James draws a dark family tree: desire becomes pregnant, gives birth to sin, and the grown-up child bears death. Three verses later he uses a birth word again for God: "It was his will to bring us to birth by the word of truth" (1:18; the verb apokyeo is the same as "bears death" here). There are two births and two families: one from human desire, ending in death; one from God's will, ending in new creation. Paul also links desire, sin and death (Romans 7:7-11), and "the wages of sin" is death in Romans 6:23.

a: All good giving and every complete gift
p: In Greek the first words of the verse scan as a line of epic verse, perhaps a known saying.
b: Pasa dosis agathe kai pan dorema teleion falls into the rhythm of a Greek hexameter, the meter of Homer. It may be a proverb James quotes, or simply his care for sound. The two words for gift differ a little: dosis is the act of giving, dorema the thing given. Both come from God. "Complete" is teleios again (see the note at 1:4).
orig: πᾶσα δόσις ἀγαθὴ καὶ πᾶν δώρημα τέλειον

p: God made the sun, moon and stars, which change and cast shadows. He does not.
b: "The lights" are the heavenly bodies of Genesis 1:16: "God made the two big lights... and the stars." Psalm 136:7 praises the one "who made the big lights". The sun and moon rise, set, wax and wane, and the shadows they cast move with them. God, their maker, has "no shifting, no shadow cast by turning". The point is that God is always the giver of good, never the source of temptation (1:13).

a: bring us to birth by the word of truth
t: New birth, or a new creation?
p: Does James mean the new birth of believers, or God creating humankind (or Israel) by his word?
b: (1) Most Christian readers see the new birth of believers through the message of the good news, like 1 Peter 1:23 ("The seed it came from... God's word, which is alive and remains") and John 3:3. The Lutheran Apology of the Augsburg Confession reads it this way, as proof that James teaches new birth through the gospel and not by works. (2) Others hear an echo of creation: God made all things by his word (Genesis 1), and humans are the first share of his creatures. (3) Some Jewish-Christian readings think of Israel, called "the first of his produce" (Jeremiah 2:3). "Firstfruits" fits all three, since the first share promises the rest of the harvest.

p: The first and best of the harvest was given to God as a pledge of the whole.
b: The law told Israel: "The first and best of the early crops of your ground you are to bring to the house of the LORD your God" (Exodus 23:19). The firstfruits belonged to God and promised that the rest of the harvest would follow. Jeremiah calls Israel "the first of his produce" (Jeremiah 2:3), and Paul calls the risen Christ "the firstfruits" of the dead (1 Corinthians 15:20). James' readers are God's first share of a world he means to renew.

a: ready to listen, slow to talk, slow to anger
p: A saying of Jewish wisdom, joined to the description of God himself, "slow to anger".
b: Sirach 5:11 says: "Be quick in your listening, and give your answer with patience." Proverbs warns that a quick talker is worse off than a fool (Proverbs 29:20). "Slow to anger" is how God described himself to Moses (Exodus 34:6: "slow to anger, great in loyal love"). James' three commands set the plan for much of the letter: listening that turns into doing (1:22-25), controlling the tongue (1:26; 3:1-12), and putting away anger and quarrels (1:20; 4:1-2).

p: Here it means the right life God wants, not Paul's gift of righteousness from God.
b: Paul uses "God's righteousness" for God's saving act revealed in the good news (Romans 1:17). In James the phrase means the right conduct that God requires and approves. Human anger, however justified it feels, does not produce that kind of life. The same Greek words can carry different meanings in different writers, which matters for reading James 2 beside Paul (see the note at 2:14).

a: the word that has been rooted in you
p: Emphytos means planted in, or inborn. James means the word of truth that gave them new birth.
b: Emphytos was used in Greek thought for something natural or inborn. Here it cannot simply mean inborn, since the readers must "accept" it. Most read it as the message of truth planted in them at their new birth (1:18), like seed in soil (compare Jesus' parable of the sower, Mark 4:14-20). Others hear Jeremiah's promise: "I will put my law inside them, and on their hearts I will write it" (Jeremiah 31:33). The two may be one idea: the word James has in mind is also "the complete law" (1:25).

p: Psyche means the whole living self, not only the part that survives death.
b: Psychas can be rendered "souls" or "lives". In Jewish usage it is the whole person. James is thinking of the final judgment (2:13-14; 5:20, "will save his soul from death"), so "save your souls" means rescue you, your whole self, on the last day.

p: James echoes Jesus' house on the rock and Paul's "doers of the law".
b: Jesus ended the Sermon on the Mount with two builders: the one who "listens to these words of mine and acts on them", and the one who "does not act on them" (Matthew 7:24, 26). Paul says the same thing in Romans 2:13: "Hearing the law does not make people righteous with God. It is the doers of the law who will be justified." In a culture where Scripture was heard read aloud in the synagogue, the danger James names was real: to hear every week and go home unchanged.

p: Mirrors were polished bronze. James' man glances, then forgets.
b: Ancient mirrors were polished metal and showed a dim picture, as Paul says: "For now we look through a mirror, and what we see is a riddle" (1 Corinthians 13:12). James' point is not that the mirror is poor but that the looker is careless: he glances (katanoeo) and walks off. The face "he was born with" is literally "the face of his birth" (genesis). The contrast in 1:25 is between this quick glance and the one who "bends close to look" into the law and stays there.

a: the complete law, the law of freedom
t: What is the law of freedom?
p: James means God's law, but which law, and why "freedom"?
b: (1) The Torah itself, as many Jews spoke of it: "The LORD's law is flawless; it brings the soul back to life" (Psalm 19:7), a law that sets free rather than enslaves. (2) The law as Jesus taught it, summed up in the royal law of love (2:8), which James also calls "a law of freedom" (2:12). (3) The message of the gospel, the "word" of 1:18-23. Luther, in his 1522 preface, set James' "law of liberty" against Paul, who calls the law "a law of slavery, of wrath, of death, and of sin". Many readers today think James and Paul both mean the law as fulfilled in love (Galatians 5:14; Romans 13:9).

p: Threskeia means outward worship: prayers, fasts, offerings, rites.
b: Threskos and threskeia describe religious practice that can be seen. Acts 26:5 uses threskeia for the Pharisees' strict way of worship. James does not reject such worship. He says a worshiper who cannot control his tongue fools himself, and he redefines the true worship God accepts in the next verse.

p: The law and the prophets name orphans and widows as the people God himself defends.
b: Moses says God "sees that the orphan and the widow get justice" (Deuteronomy 10:18), and Isaiah tells Israel: "Give the orphan his rights; take up the widow's case" (Isaiah 1:17). Without a husband or father, a woman and her children had no one to speak for them at law and often no income. James' "to visit" (episkeptesthai) is the word for looking after the sick and needy, and also for God's own coming to help his people (Luke 1:68). The early church cared for widows from the start (Acts 6:1; 1 Timothy 5:3-16).
r: Deuteronomy 10:18; Deuteronomy 14:29; Isaiah 1:17; Acts 6:1; 1 Timothy 5:3-16; Matthew 25:36

p: Prosopolempsia comes from a Hebrew idiom: to "lift up" or "receive" someone's face, that is, to judge by appearances.
b: The Greek word is built from "face" and "receive", from the Hebrew idiom in Leviticus 19:15: "Do not lift up the face of the poor man, and do not honor the face of the great man. Judge your fellow citizen in what is right." God "does not play favorites" (Deuteronomy 10:17), and Paul says: "For with God there are no favorites" (Romans 2:11). Leviticus 19 lies behind this whole chapter: 19:15 here, 19:18 in 2:8.

a: the faith of Jesus Christ, our Lord of glory
p: "The faith of Jesus Christ" and the loose words "of glory" can each be read more than one way.
b: (1) "The faith of Jesus Christ" may mean faith in him, or the faith he himself had and taught, as with Paul's pistis Christou (see the notes at Romans 3:22 and Galatians 2:16). (2) The Greek ends with "of glory" after the name: tou kyriou hemon Iesou Christou tes doxes. It may mean "our glorious Lord", "our Lord of glory" (as "the Lord of glory", 1 Corinthians 2:8), or "Jesus Christ, the Glory", that is, the glory of God's presence come among people. This is one of the two places James names Jesus (with 1:1). Luther complained that James "names Christ several times" but "teaches nothing about him". Many readers answer that a letter which calls Jesus "the Lord of glory" in passing assumes a high faith its readers already shared. The SBL edition prints the verse as a question.
orig: τὴν πίστιν τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τῆς δόξης

p: James calls the believers' meeting a synagoge, the word for a Jewish assembly and its building.
b: This is the only place in the New Testament where a Christian meeting is called a synagogue (in 5:14 James says "church", ekklesia). The word suggests Jewish believers who still met as a synagogue of their own. Readers take the scene in two ways. (1) A meeting for worship and teaching, where seating showed rank. (2) A meeting where the church judged disputes between members, as Jewish communities did: in 1969 Roy Bowen Ward argued that James describes such a judicial assembly, which would explain "judges" in 2:4 and the courts in 2:6. The IVP New Testament Commentary, which weighs both, calls his view "intriguing but not conclusive".

p: The same verb as the doubter's wavering in 1:6.
b: Diekrithete is the verb of 1:6, where the man who asks God for wisdom must not "waver". A church that sorts people by their clothes has become divided inside, like the double-minded man. The "judges whose reasoning is wicked" are judges who decide by money and rank, which the law of Moses forbids (Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 1:17).

a: poor as the world counts it
p: James echoes Jesus' first beatitude and Paul's words on God's choice of the lowly.
b: In Luke, Jesus says: "Blessed are the poor, because the kingdom of God is yours" (Luke 6:20); Matthew has "poor in spirit" (Matthew 5:3). Paul writes that "God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise" (1 Corinthians 1:27). In the Psalms and prophets "the poor" are often the humble faithful who depend on God (the anawim). James joins both senses: poor in what the world counts, rich in faith, heirs of the kingdom promised "to those who love him" (as in 1:12).

p: Rich people were taking the readers to court.
b: The verb helko means to drag, as Paul and Silas were hauled before the rulers at Philippi (Acts 16:19). James finds it absurd that a church should honor the very class that treats its members this way. The same rich appear in 5:1-6, holding back wages.

a: the good name that was pronounced over you
p: An Old Testament way of saying "you belong to him", probably spoken at baptism.
b: "The LORD's name has been called over you" marked Israel as God's own people (Deuteronomy 28:10). James himself quotes the same idiom in Acts 15:17: "all the nations over whom my name has been called". Here the name is most likely Jesus' name, spoken over each believer at baptism (Acts 2:38; 22:16). Those who insult it insult the one the believers belong to.

p: Nomos basilikos: the law of the King, or the law that rules all the others.
b: "You are to love your neighbor as yourself" comes from Leviticus 19:18. It is "royal" either because it belongs to the King and his kingdom (2:5), or because it rules over the other commands, as Jesus said: "The whole law hangs from these two commandments" (Matthew 22:40). Paul too says the whole law "stands fulfilled in a single saying" (Galatians 5:14). James' point is sharp: favoring the rich breaks the very command people think they are keeping.

p: Breaking one command makes you a lawbreaker, since one God gave them all.
b: The Mishnah, compiled about AD 200, records the saying: "be careful with a light commandment as with a grave one" (Avot 2:1). Paul warns the Galatians that a man who gets circumcised becomes "bound to do the whole law" (Galatians 5:3). James does not say that every sin is equally bad. He says the law hangs together, because the same God spoke every part of it (2:11). So no one can excuse favoritism by pointing to the commands he keeps.

p: James puts adultery first, as the Greek Bible and other New Testament lists often do.
b: In the Hebrew text of the Ten Commandments murder comes before adultery (Exodus 20:13-14; Deuteronomy 5:17-18). In Codex Vaticanus, the main manuscript of the Greek Old Testament, adultery comes first in both places, and the same order is found in Luke 18:20 and Romans 13:9 ("Do not commit adultery," "Do not murder"). James quotes in the order his Greek Bible had. The choice of murder may also prepare for 4:2 ("You murder") and 5:6.

p: The merciful will meet mercy at the judgment. Jesus taught the same.
b: "Blessed are the merciful, because mercy will be shown to them" (Matthew 5:7). The unforgiving servant of Matthew 18:23-35 is the picture of "judgment with no mercy for the one who showed none". Hosea's "Loyal love is what I want, not sacrifice" (Hosea 6:6) stands behind it. The verb katakauchatai means to boast over, to triumph: in the end mercy has the last word over strict judgment.

t: What James means by faith and works
p: James and Paul use the same words, faith, works, justify, but not always in the same sense.
b: In 2:14-26 "faith" is the faith a person "claims" to have: believing that God is one, which even demons do (2:19). "Works" are deeds of mercy, clothing and feeding a brother or sister (2:15-16), and acts of trust such as Abraham's and Rahab's. Paul, when he writes "a person is justified by faith, apart from works of the law" (Romans 3:28), means by faith a trust that joins a person to Christ, and by "works of the law" the deeds the Torah required (some think chiefly the marks of Jewish identity, such as circumcision, food laws and the Sabbath). Readers who set the two side by side should keep these differences in view. The chapter page gives how the churches have read the passage.

a: That kind of faith cannot save him, can it?
p: The Greek has the article: "the faith", that is, the faith just described.
b: The question is me dynatai he pistis sosai auton, a question that expects the answer "no". The article "the" points back to the faith someone "claims" but does not show. James does not ask whether faith saves, but whether this faith, words without deeds, can save. "Save" here looks to the final judgment (2:12-13).
orig: μὴ δύναται ἡ πίστις σῶσαι αὐτόν;

t: A blessing with nothing in it
p: "Go in peace" was a normal Jewish farewell and blessing.
b: The priest of Judges 18:6 and Eli in 1 Samuel 1:17 send people off with "Go in peace". Here the blessing is empty, because the speaker could have given food and clothing and did not. "Stay warm" and "get enough to eat" may be read as commands or as wishes. James' picture is like 1 John 3:17, which asks how God's love can live in someone who sees a brother in need and shuts his heart.

t: Where do the objector's words end?
p: Greek had no quotation marks, and readers disagree on how much of the verse the imagined speaker says.
b: James uses the style of the diatribe, a teacher's argument with an imagined opponent. (1) The objector says only "You have faith, and I have works", meaning "faith and works are different gifts; you have one, I have the other"; James replies "Show me your faith...". This is how the Plain English Translation punctuates it. Printed editions and translations differ on where the quotation ends. (2) The speaker is an ally of James, saying "You (claim to) have faith, and I have works". (3) The objector's words run on to the end of the verse, or into 2:19. The general sense is clear whichever is right: faith cannot be shown without deeds.
orig: Ἀλλ’ ἐρεῖ τις· Σὺ πίστιν ἔχεις κἀγὼ ἔργα ἔχω

a: You believe that God is one
p: James cites Israel's central confession, which every Jew said daily.
b: "Listen, Israel: The LORD is our God. The LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Jesus called it the first command (Mark 12:29). James praises the confession ("Fine") and then shows that correct belief alone is not the faith that saves: the demons hold it too, and it makes them shake with fear (compare the demon's cry in Mark 5:7). The next words of the Shema are "Love the LORD your God" (Deuteronomy 6:5), and love is what the demons lack.

a: faith without the works is idle
p: A pun: faith choris ton ergon (without works) is arge (without work, idle).
b: Arge is a-erge, "not working", the word for an idle worker or land left fallow (Matthew 20:3, 6). James plays on erga: faith without works does no work. Many later manuscripts read "dead" here, as in 2:17 and 2:26; see the variant. "Empty man" (kene) means a man hollow inside, with words but nothing behind them.

p: Jewish tradition before James counted the binding of Isaac as the test in which Abraham's faith was proved.
b: In Genesis 22:1 "God put Abraham to the test", and he did not hold back his son (Genesis 22:12). The binding of Isaac (the Akedah) became for Jewish teachers the greatest of Abraham's trials. 1 Maccabees joins it to the words of Genesis 15:6 just as James does: "Abraham: was he not found faithful in the test, and was it not reckoned to him as righteousness?" (1 Maccabees 2:52). Sirach 44:20 says that "in testing he was found faithful". James stands in this tradition. Paul, using the same Abraham, asks a different question: "If Abraham was justified by works, he has a reason to boast, though not with God" (Romans 4:2).

p: Dikaioo means to declare or show someone to be in the right. Readers differ on whose verdict James means.
b: (1) God's verdict at the last judgment, which takes account of a person's deeds (2:12-13; Matthew 12:37: "It is by your words that you will be justified"). (2) The showing that someone is truly righteous: Calvin says James "is speaking of the manifestation, not of the imputation of righteousness". (3) Being made righteous: John Wesley's note says Abraham was justified "in St. James's sense, (that is, made righteous,) by works, consequent to his faith", and in Paul's sense "accounted righteous" by faith. Catholic teaching speaks of justification increasing through faith working with good works (Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 10, which quotes 2:24). The chapter page's card gives each church's view.

a: the works made his faith complete
p: Eteleiothe: faith was completed, reached its end, by what Abraham did.
b: The verb is from teleios, "complete" (see 1:4). James does not say works replaced faith. He says faith "was at work along with" the works (synergei, "worked together") and was completed by them, as a promise is completed when it is kept. Hebrews 11:17 says Abraham offered Isaac "by faith".

a: Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness
p: James quotes the verse Paul builds on, and says the binding of Isaac fulfilled it.
b: Genesis 15:6 reads in the Hebrew: "Abram put his trust in the LORD, and he reckoned it to him as righteousness." James quotes the Greek form, the same words as Romans 4:3: "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness." Paul uses the verse to show that Abraham was counted righteous before he did anything (Romans 4:9-10). James says the verse "came true" (eplerothe, was fulfilled) years later at the altar, when his trust was proved in action. Luther judged this reading of Genesis 15 indefensible in his 1522 preface; Wesley's notes, by contrast, see two moments of justification.

p: The title comes from 2 Chronicles 20:7 and Isaiah 41:8.
b: Jehoshaphat prays: "You gave it for all time to the offspring of your friend Abraham" (2 Chronicles 20:7). In Isaiah 41:8 the Hebrew 'ohavi is rendered on this site "offspring of Abraham, who loved me"; it can also be read as "my friend". For James the title fits the contrast he will draw in 4:4: friendship with the world, or friendship with God.

t: The only "faith alone" in the Bible
p: The words "faith alone" occur in the Bible only here, where James denies that a person is justified by faith alone.
b: The Greek ouk ek pisteos monon is exact: "not by faith only". No other verse of the Bible joins "faith" and "alone" (Jesus' "only believe", Mark 5:36, is a different phrase). The Council of Trent quoted this verse when it taught that justification increases as "faith co-operating with good works". The Lutheran Apology of the Augsburg Confession said of its opponents' use of 2:24, "Nor is any other passage supposed to be more contrary to our belief," and answered that James speaks of the works that follow living faith. Reformed and Wesleyan readers likewise distinguish the faith that justifies from the claim to faith that James attacks. The chapter page sets these views side by side.
orig: οὐκ ἐκ πίστεως μόνον (ouk ek pisteos monon)

p: James' second example is a Canaanite woman, the opposite of Abraham in almost every way.
b: The spies "came to the house of a prostitute named Rahab" (Joshua 2:1). She hid them, let them down "by a rope through the window" (Joshua 2:15) and sent them off by the hill road. Hebrews 11:31 praises her faith: "By faith Rahab the prostitute was not destroyed along with the disobedient, since she had taken in the spies in peace." Matthew names her among Jesus' ancestors (Matthew 1:5). James calls the spies "messengers" (angelous); a few manuscripts change it to "spies". Abraham, the patriarch, and Rahab, the foreign outsider, are justified the same way.

p: Pneuma is spirit and breath. A body without it is a corpse.
b: The picture goes back to Genesis 2:7, where God "blew into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living being". James compares faith to the body and works to the breath that makes it live. The comparison is pointed: one might expect faith to be the spirit and works the body, but James turns it around, so that works are the sign that faith is alive.

a: do not let many of you become teachers
p: Teachers held honor in the early church. James warns that the honor brings a stricter judgment.
b: Teachers are named among the church's gifts (Acts 13:1; 1 Corinthians 12:28). Jesus warned his followers against seeking the title: "Your Teacher is one, and you are all brothers" (Matthew 23:8). James includes himself ("we will receive"), since teachers work with words, and words are what the rest of the chapter is about. Jesus said: "every idle word people say, they will have to answer for on judgment day" (Matthew 12:36).

p: Teleios again: the goal of 1:4, reached by the one who masters his tongue.
b: In 1:4 James wanted his readers to be "complete and whole". Here he names one test of it: never tripping in speech. He does not claim anyone reaches it ("All of us trip up in many ways"). The verb "bridle" picks up 1:26, where the religious man who does not bridle his tongue has an empty religion, and leads into the horses of 3:3.

p: Small things that steer or burn large things: three pictures of the tongue's power.
b: James gives three pictures of a small thing with great power: the bit that turns a horse, the rudder that steers a ship, and the small flame that sets a forest on fire. The psalmist promised to put a muzzle on his own mouth: "I will watch how I go, and keep my tongue from sin. My mouth will wear a muzzle" (Psalm 39:1). Proverbs says: "Death and life are in the tongue's hand" (Proverbs 18:21).

p: The Greek uses one word, helikos, for both the small fire and the great forest.
b: Idou helikon pyr helikēn hylēn anaptei, literally "look, how great a fire, how great a forest it kindles". Helikos can mean "how great" or "how small", so the line plays on size: a fire this small, a forest this large. Many manuscripts read oligon, "a little" fire, which spells out the sense (see the variant). The Plain English Translation takes the first helikos as "how small", because the line sets it against the great forest. Sirach 28:12 has a similar picture of the mouth: "If you blow on a spark, it will blaze; if you spit on it, it will go out; and both come out of your mouth."
orig: ἡλίκον πῦρ ἡλίκην ὕλην (helikon pyr helikēn hylēn)

p: The Greek of 3:6 is one of the most tangled in the letter, and editors punctuate it differently.
b: The words run: "and the tongue a fire, the world of injustice, the tongue is set among our members, staining..." Is "the world of injustice" a second name for the tongue (a whole world of evil in one small member), or the subject of a new sentence? Is "is set" (kathistatai) "is placed" or "makes itself"? The Byzantine text adds "so" (houtos, KJV "so is the tongue") to smooth it. The Plain English Translation takes "a world of injustice" as a description of the tongue and "placed among our members" as what follows, one of the ways editors and translators punctuate it.
orig: ὁ κόσμος τῆς ἀδικίας ἡ γλῶσσα καθίσταται ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν ἡμῶν

p: Ton trochon tes geneseos: literally "the wheel of birth (or of becoming)". What it means is debated.
b: Trochos is a wheel; genesis is birth, origin or existence (the same word as "the face he was born with", 1:23). (1) The whole course of a human life, the wheel set turning at birth: Albert Barnes explained it as "the wheel which is set in motion at birth, and which runs on through life". (2) The whole round of creation, "the orb of creation", as Ellicott put it, so that the tongue sets the world on fire. The KJV's "the course of nature" is close to the first two readings. The Plain English Translation keeps the picture of a wheel so readers can weigh it.
orig: τὸν τροχὸν τῆς γενέσεως (ton trochon tes geneseos)

p: The usual English "hell" hides a place name: the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem.
b: Gehenna is the Greek form of Ge-Hinnom, the Valley of Hinnom on the south side of Jerusalem, where children had once been burned as offerings (Jeremiah 7:31) and which became a picture of final judgment by fire. Outside the Gospels the word appears only here. Jesus had warned that calling a brother "You idiot!" makes a person "liable to the fire of Gehenna" (Matthew 5:22). James turns it around: the tongue that burns others is itself lit from Gehenna.

p: James lists the creatures in the four groups of Genesis.
b: Wild animals, birds, creeping things and sea creatures are the four classes of Genesis 1:26 and 9:2 ("every wild animal of the earth and every bird of the sky... everything that creeps on the ground and all the fish of the sea"). Humankind was told to rule them, and has. Yet the small member inside its own mouth will not be ruled.

p: The Psalms compare slanderers' tongues to snakes.
b: "They whet their tongues like a snake; under their lips lies the venom of the viper" (Psalm 140:3, quoted by Paul in Romans 3:13). "Poison" is ios, the same word James uses for the "rust" that eats the rich man's gold in 5:3. "Unsettled" (akatastaton) echoes the "unsteady" double-minded man of 1:8 (akatastatos).

a: who came into being after God's likeness
p: To curse a human being is to curse someone made like God.
b: "Let us make humankind in our image, as our likeness" (Genesis 1:26). After the flood God forbids murder for the same reason: "in God's image he made humankind" (Genesis 9:6). James applies it to speech: the mouth that blesses God cannot curse the people who bear his likeness. Jesus taught his followers to bless and pray even for enemies (Matthew 5:44; Luke 6:28).

p: Jewish prayer is full of blessings of God. James' readers blessed God in their prayers every day.
b: To "bless" God (eulogeo, Hebrew barakh) is to praise and thank him, as Job does: "Let the LORD's name be blessed" (Job 1:21). Jewish prayer was built on such blessings, and Christians kept the form (2 Corinthians 1:3; Ephesians 1:3; 1 Peter 1:3, "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ"). "The Lord and Father" is a title found nowhere else in the New Testament in this form; many later manuscripts read "God and Father" (see the variant).

a: a fig tree cannot grow olives
p: Jesus used the same kind of picture about prophets.
b: "You will know who they are from their fruit. Does anyone gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?" (Matthew 7:16). Fig, olive and vine were the three great crops of the land of Israel. The point in James: speech shows what kind of source a person is, and a single spring cannot pour out two kinds of water.

p: The phrase comes from Deuteronomy, where wisdom is shown by keeping God's rules.
b: Moses tells Israel that keeping the law will make the nations say, "This great nation is surely a wise and understanding people!" (Deuteronomy 4:6; compare Deuteronomy 1:13). For James too wisdom is shown, not claimed: "let his good life show his works". "Gentleness" (prautes) is the same quality asked of the hearer in 1:21; it is the opposite of the self-promoting "wisdom" of 3:14-16.

p: A word for self-seeking ambition, the spirit of a person who campaigns for himself.
b: Eritheia may come from a word for hired labor or from canvassing for office; in the New Testament it is the spirit that pushes oneself forward and splits a group into parties. Paul lists it among the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:20, "selfish ambition") and warns, "Do nothing to push yourselves forward" (Philippians 2:3). James pairs it with "bitter jealousy" (zelos, which could also be the "zeal" of a religious party).

p: Psychike: belonging to the natural, unspiritual person, the same word as Jude 1:19.
b: The adjective comes from psyche, "soul" or natural life. Paul writes: "A natural person does not welcome the things of the Spirit of God" (1 Corinthians 2:14), and Jude says of the intruders: "They are merely natural and lack the Spirit" (Jude 1:19). James' three steps go downward: earthly, merely natural, demonic. Wisdom that serves the self ends up serving the demons who "believe" (2:19) but do not obey.

p: James' list is like Jewish lists of Wisdom's qualities, and like Paul's fruit of the Spirit.
b: The Wisdom of Solomon (part of the Bible for Catholic and Orthodox Christians) lists more than twenty marks of Wisdom, among them "holy", "unstained" and "kind to humankind" (Wisdom of Solomon 7:22-23). Paul names "the Spirit's fruit" (Galatians 5:22-23). For James wisdom does almost what the Spirit does in Paul: it comes "from above" (1:5, 17) and produces peace. "Unwavering" (adiakritos) may mean "impartial", that is, not playing favorites (2:1-4), or "undivided", not double-minded (1:6-8); James may intend both.

p: "Blessed are the peacemakers" (Matthew 5:9).
b: Jesus said: "Blessed are the peacemakers, because they will be called sons of God" (Matthew 5:9). Isaiah promised: "What righteousness makes will be peace" (Isaiah 32:17). James joins the two: righteousness is a harvest, and it grows only from seed sown in peace, by peacemakers. The verse is the bridge into chapter 4, which opens with wars and fights.

p: Hedonai: the pleasures that people crave, here pictured as soldiers fighting inside them.
b: The word gives English "hedonism". James pictures the pleasures as an army camped in "your body's members", at war with each other and with the soul. 1 Peter 2:11 uses the same picture: "keep away from the flesh's desires. They are at war with the soul." The outer wars and fights in the church come from the inner war in each person.

p: "You murder" is startling in a letter to believers. Readers take it as hyperbole, as fact, or as a hypothetical.
b: (1) Most read it as strong language for hatred, as Jesus treated anger as a form of murder (Matthew 5:21-22; compare 1 John 3:15). (2) Some take it literally, of members drawn into the violence of the years before the Jewish revolt, or of the rich who "killed" the righteous (5:6). (3) The punctuation also matters: the Plain English Translation follows the SBL edition, where each lack leads to a violent act ("You want and do not have. You murder..."). Other editions place the stops differently, but every reading ends in the same diagnosis: "The reason you do not have is that you do not ask."

a: you ask in a bad way
p: James comes back to the asking of 1:5-6: God gives freely, but not to fund pleasures.
b: Jesus promised that asking would be answered (Matthew 7:7), and James has already said that God gives "with an open hand" (1:5). The problem is not God's unwillingness but the asker: he wants to "pour it out" (dapanao, to spend, the word for the prodigal son's spending in Luke 15:14) on his own pleasures. Prayer that serves the self is not the prayer of faith (5:15).

p: The prophets pictured God's people as a wife who left her husband. James uses that picture.
b: Hosea's marriage to an unfaithful wife stood for Israel's going after other gods (Hosea 2:2, "for she is not my wife, and I am not her husband"). Jeremiah says: "as a woman betrays her companion, so you have betrayed me, house of Israel" (Jeremiah 3:20). James' feminine plural ("adulteresses") shows he means this picture, not literal adultery: the church is God's bride, and loving the world is unfaithfulness to him. Jesus called his generation "adulterous" in the same sense (Matthew 12:39). Many later manuscripts add "adulterers and" (KJV): see the variant.

a: being the world's friend means being God's enemy
p: Abraham was "the friend of God" (2:23). James' readers must choose whose friend to be.
b: "The world" in James is the way of life organized against God: its stains (1:27), its values that honor the rich (2:5), its earthly wisdom (3:15). Jesus said: "You cannot be a slave both to God and to wealth" (Matthew 6:24). In the ancient world friendship meant shared loyalties; one could not be the friend of a man and of his enemy. 1 John 2:15 warns, "Do not love the world."

p: No verse of the Old Testament says what James quotes in 4:5. Where did it come from?
b: James introduces the words as Scripture, yet they match no known verse. (1) He sums up a theme rather than a verse: God is jealous for his people (Exodus 20:5, "I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God"; Exodus 34:14). (2) He quotes a writing now lost, or one his readers knew outside our Bible. (3) The quotation is really the Proverbs line in 4:6, and 4:5b is James' own comment. None of these is certain. The reading the Plain English Translation follows is explained in the next note.

a: With jealousy he yearns for the spirit he placed to live in us
p: Who yearns, God or the human spirit? And is the "spirit" the human spirit or the Holy Spirit?
b: The Greek is pros phthonon epipothei to pneuma ho katokisen en hemin. (1) God yearns jealously for the spirit he made to live in us, that is, for his people's whole devotion. This fits the jealous husband of 4:4 and is followed by the Plain English Translation. (2) The human spirit that God placed in us longs enviously; this fits 4:1-2 ("you envy") and is the KJV's reading ("The spirit that dwelleth in us lusteth to envy"). (3) The Holy Spirit whom God made to live in us yearns jealously over us. Against (1), phthonos is normally a bad word, "envy", not the "jealousy" (zelos) the Greek Bible uses of God. For it, James may have chosen a strong word on purpose. A variant (katokesen, "that lives") is given separately.
orig: πρὸς φθόνον ἐπιποθεῖ τὸ πνεῦμα ὃ κατῴκισεν ἐν ἡμῖν

a: God takes his stand against the proud, but to the humble he gives grace
p: James quotes the Greek of Proverbs 3:34, as 1 Peter 5:5 also does, word for word.
b: The Hebrew of Proverbs 3:34 reads, on this site: "Mockers he mocks, but the humble he gives his favor." The Greek translation turned it into "The Lord opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble", and James quotes that Greek, with "God" for "the Lord". 1 Peter 5:5 quotes it in exactly the same form as James: "God takes his stand against the proud, but to the humble he gives grace." The verb antitassetai is military: to line up in battle against someone. Grace, the gift no one earned, goes to those who know they need it.
orig: ὁ θεὸς ὑπερηφάνοις ἀντιτάσσεται, ταπεινοῖς δὲ δίδωσιν χάριν

a: Stand up against the devil, and he will run away from you
p: 1 Peter 5:8-9 gives the same command after the same Proverbs quotation.
b: Both James and 1 Peter follow Proverbs 3:34 with a call to humble oneself before God and to resist the devil (1 Peter 5:5-9). The likeness suggests a pattern of teaching the early church shared. Jesus himself resisted the devil with Scripture in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1-11), and Ephesians 6:11-13 tells believers to "stand".

a: Come close to God, and he will come close to you
t: Return to me, and I will return to you
p: James echoes the prophets' call to return, and the priestly language of clean hands.
b: Zechariah 1:3 and Malachi 3:7 promise: "Return to me, and I will return to you." "Come close" (engizo) was a word for priests approaching God's altar, and "clean your hands" and "make your hearts pure" recall the psalm of who may go up to the LORD's mountain: "Someone whose hands are clean and whose heart is pure" (Psalm 24:4). The "double-minded" are again the divided people of 1:8.

a: Let your laughing be turned into grief
p: Jesus' woe in Luke 6:25, turned into a call to repent.
b: "Woe, you who are laughing now, because you will grieve and weep" (Luke 6:25). James turns the woe into an invitation: grieve now, by your own choice, over your sin, and God will lift you (4:10). This is the language of Israel's days of fasting and repentance (Joel 2:12-13).

a: Make yourselves low before the Lord, and he will raise you high
p: James returns to the reversal of 1:9-10, in the words of Jesus.
b: "Anyone who raises himself up will be brought low, and anyone who brings himself low will be raised up" (Matthew 23:12). 1 Peter 5:6 also says: "So let yourselves be brought low under God's strong hand, so that he can lift you high at the right time." The "lowly brother" of 1:9 who is "raised high" is the model.

p: Katalaleo is to speak against someone, often behind his back. James says it puts the speaker above the law.
b: The law itself forbids it: "Do not go about as a slanderer among your kin" (Leviticus 19:16), in the same chapter as "love your neighbor" (Leviticus 19:18), the royal law of 2:8. To slander a brother is to break that law, and so to act as if the law did not apply to you. That makes you the law's judge instead of its doer (1:22-25).

a: Only one is Lawgiver and Judge
p: Only God gives the law and judges by it, and only he can save and destroy.
b: "For the LORD is our judge, the LORD is our commander, the LORD is our king" (Isaiah 33:22). God says: "I kill, and I make alive... and no one can pull anyone out of my hand" (Deuteronomy 32:39). "One" echoes the Shema (2:19). Jesus said that God has power to destroy both body and soul in Gehenna (Matthew 10:28). Many later manuscripts lack "and Judge" (see the variant).

a: buy and sell, and turn a profit
p: James addresses traders who plan a year's business in another city.
b: Traders moved from city to city with their goods; Aquila and Priscilla, Jews who had come from Italy, set up their trade in Corinth (Acts 18:2-3). James does not condemn trade. He condemns planning as if God did not exist. Jesus told of a rich man who planned bigger barns and died that night (Luke 12:16-21).

a: You are a puff of steam
p: Human life is brief, as the Psalms and Proverbs say.
b: "Every human being, even standing firm, is nothing but a puff of air" (Psalm 39:5). "Don't brag about tomorrow, since you cannot know what a day will give birth to" (Proverbs 27:1). Atmis is vapor: steam, mist, or a haze of smoke ("blood and fire and a haze of smoke", Acts 2:19, quoting Joel). The Plain English Translation says "steam" for the picture of vapor that rises and is gone. Hosea says faithless Israel will be "like the morning cloud... like smoke from a window" (Hosea 13:3).

p: Paul writes the same way about his travel plans.
b: Paul tells the Ephesians, "I will turn back to you again, God willing" (Acts 18:21), and the Corinthians, "I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills" (1 Corinthians 4:19). Christians later shortened the phrase in Latin to Deo volente. For James the words are not a charm but an honest admission that every plan depends on God.
orig: ἐὰν ὁ κύριος θελήσῃ (ean ho kyrios thelese)

p: Not doing the good you know is sin too.
b: James ends the section with a short rule that sums up the letter's concern with doing. Christian teaching came to call this a sin of omission: what is left undone. Jesus told of the slave "who knew what his master wanted, yet neither made ready nor acted on his master's wishes" (Luke 12:47), and of the people who did not feed or clothe him (Matthew 25:41-46).

a: Now then, you who are rich
p: James speaks to the rich as the prophets spoke to the nations, people outside the listening church.
b: The section reads like a prophet's woe oracle. Most readers think the rich landowners are not church members: James does not call them "brothers", offers no call to repent, and turns to his readers in 5:7 ("So, brothers"). The woe was for the poor believers to hear, a promise that God sees. Others think rich members are included, as a warning. Jesus said: "But woe to you who are rich, because your comfort is already paid to you in full" (Luke 6:24).

a: Your clothes are full of moth holes
p: James echoes Jesus' words about treasure on earth.
b: "Do not pile up treasures for yourselves on earth. Here moths and rust eat them away" (Matthew 6:19). In the ancient world fine clothing was a store of wealth, like gold and grain. James speaks as if the judgment has already happened: the riches "have gone rotten" (perfect tense), the clothes are already moth-eaten.

p: Gold does not rust. James means that hoarded wealth is ruined, and he chooses the same word as "poison" in 3:8.
b: Gold and silver do not corrode as iron does, which makes the picture deliberate: wealth kept out of use while workers go unpaid is already ruined in God's sight. The word ios means both rust and venom (3:8, "poison that kills"), and here the rust becomes a witness in court and then a fire that eats flesh. "You piled up treasure" is the verb of Matthew 6:19, and "in the last days" adds the irony: they stored up wealth when the end was near.

a: The pay of the laborers who cut your fields
p: The law of Moses required a day laborer to be paid the same day.
b: "Pay him his wages each day, before the sun goes down, because he is poor and his heart is set on it. Otherwise he will cry out to the LORD against you" (Deuteronomy 24:15). "The wages of a hired worker must not stay with you overnight" (Leviticus 19:13). Malachi 3:5 lists among those God will judge "those who cheat a hired worker of his pay". Seasonal reapers in the land of Israel were often landless men hired by the day, as in Jesus' parable (Matthew 20:1-16).

p: Kyrios sabaoth keeps the Hebrew word for armies: the God who commands the hosts of heaven.
b: Sabaoth is the Hebrew tseva'ot, "armies", left untranslated in the Greek, as in Romans 9:29. This site renders the Old Testament title "the LORD of Armies" and the Greek form "the Lord of Armies". James seems to echo Isaiah 5:9, a woe on rich landowners: "In my ears the LORD of Armies has spoken." The cries of unpaid workers reach the ears of the commander of heaven's armies.

p: The rich are like cattle fattening themselves on the day they are to be killed.
b: Jeremiah prayed against the wicked who prospered: "Pull them away like sheep for the slaughter. Set them aside for the day of killing" (Jeremiah 12:3). James' picture is of animals eating their fill unaware that the knife is ready. "The day of slaughter" may be the coming judgment, or the day the rich did their own slaughtering of the poor (5:6).

p: The innocent poor man in general, Jesus, or James himself? Readers have heard all three.
b: (1) Any righteous poor person ruined by the rich, as in the Wisdom of Solomon, where the wicked say: "Let us oppress the righteous poor man" (Wisdom of Solomon 2:10) and plot to condemn him to a shameful death (2:20). (2) Jesus, called "the Righteous One" in Acts 3:14 and 7:52, condemned and killed without resisting. (3) Later readers noticed that James himself was known as "the Just" (the same Greek word): Hegesippus, quoted by Eusebius, says James "has been called the Just by all". The last words can also be read as a question, "Does he not stand against you?", that is, God (or the dead man) will oppose you at the judgment.
r: Wisdom of Solomon 2:10-20; Acts 3:14; Acts 7:52; Isaiah 53:7; Matthew 5:39

p: Parousia: the arrival of a king on an official visit, used of Christ's return.
b: Parousia means presence or arrival, and was used for a ruler's visit to a city. The church used it for Jesus' return (Matthew 24:3, 27; 1 Thessalonians 4:15). "The Lord" here is most likely Jesus, as in 5:8 and in Paul's letters, though James can also use "Lord" for God (5:4, 10-11). The hope of his coming is the reason for patience: the Judge is near (5:9).

p: In the land of Israel the year's crop depended on two rains, at sowing and before harvest.
b: The law promised: "I will give your land its rain at the right time, the early rain and the late rain" (Deuteronomy 11:14). The early rain came at the start of the farming year, when the ground was plowed and sown; the late rain came before the harvest. A farmer could do nothing to hurry either. The picture is of patience that is not idle, the patience of someone who has done his work and waits for God to give the harvest. The detail suits a writer who knew the land's farming.

a: the Judge stands right outside the doors
p: Jesus said the end would be "right outside the doors".
b: "In the same way, when you see all these things, know that it is near, right outside the doors" (Matthew 24:33). The risen Jesus says in Revelation: "Look! I am standing at the door, knocking" (Revelation 3:20). James uses the picture as a warning to the church: grumbling about one another is passing judgment, and the real Judge is already at the door (compare 4:11-12).

p: The KJV's "the patience of Job" made Job a proverb. The Job of the book is not quiet, but he holds on.
b: Job argues, complains and demands an answer from God (Job 3; 23). What James praises is hypomone, endurance: Job does not let go of God. At the start he says, "The LORD gave, and the LORD took. Let the LORD's name be blessed" (Job 1:21), and at the end "the LORD turned Job's fortunes around" (Job 42:10). The "outcome the Lord gave" (telos kyriou) is that ending. Some have read it instead as "the end of the Lord", Jesus' death and resurrection, but most take it of Job.
orig: τὴν ὑπομονὴν Ἰὼβ (ten hypomonen Iob); τὸ τέλος κυρίου

a: the Lord is very tender-hearted and compassionate
p: James closes his comfort with God's own description of himself to Moses.
b: "The LORD, the LORD, a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6; compare Psalm 103:8). Polysplanchnos, "very tender-hearted", is literally "much-boweled", since the inner organs were thought to be where pity is felt. James has already used "slow to anger" from the same text (1:19).
orig: πολύσπλαγχνός ἐστιν ὁ κύριος καὶ οἰκτίρμων

p: Nearly the same words as Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount.
b: Jesus said: "do not take oaths at all. Do not swear by heaven, since it is God's throne, or by the earth" and "When you speak, say 'Yes, yes' or 'No, no'" (Matthew 5:34-35, 37). In both, the point is truthfulness: if every word is true, oaths are not needed. Some Christian groups have refused all oaths because of these verses; others hold that they forbid casual swearing, not oaths in court. The question has its card at Matthew 5:34.

p: Presbyteroi, the leaders of a local church, as in Acts.
b: Jewish towns and synagogues were led by elders, and the first churches followed the pattern (Acts 11:30; 14:23; 15:6, where James sits with "the apostles and the elders"). James calls the body "the church" (ekklesia) here, after "your synagogue" in 2:2. Whether these elders are the same as the later order of priests is one of the questions on the card at this chapter: the Council of Trent taught that they are priests ordained by a bishop; Calvin read them as the ordinary elders of a congregation.

p: Olive oil was used on wounds, and it was also a sign of God's blessing and setting apart.
b: The Good Samaritan "poured oil and wine on his wounds" (Luke 10:34), and Isaiah 1:6 speaks of wounds not "eased with oil". So some read James' anointing as medical care given with prayer. But James says it is done "in the name of the Lord" and by the elders, not by a physician, and the Twelve "anointed with oil and healed" many sick people (Mark 6:13), which suggests a sign of God's healing power. Some, such as the Wisconsin Evangelical Lutheran Synod, take the verb aleipho as the word for a medicinal use of oil. It is the ordinary word for rubbing on oil, but the Greek Old Testament also uses it for anointing priests (Numbers 3:3, "the anointed priests"), so the verb alone does not settle the question. The Greek of Vaticanus and a few other witnesses lacks "him" (see the variant). The churches' readings are on the chapter page.

p: Sozo means to rescue, heal and make whole. James means bodily healing, but the word carries more.
b: In the Gospels Jesus tells those he heals, "your faith has saved you", and this site keeps "save" there with the gloss "healed and made whole". Here too the sick person is "saved" and "raised up" (egeiro, the word for getting up from a sickbed, and also for resurrection). The word for the sick, kamnonta, means one who is worn out or weak, perhaps seriously ill.
orig: σώσει τὸν κάμνοντα (sosei ton kamnonta); ἐγερεῖ

p: "If": James does not say every sickness comes from sin, but that sins will be forgiven too.
b: Some sickness was linked to sin in Scripture (1 Corinthians 11:30; Mark 2:5-11), but Jesus denied that the man born blind was being punished: "This man did not sin, and his parents did not sin" (John 9:3). James' "if" keeps both open. He joins healing and forgiveness as Jesus did with the paralyzed man (Mark 2:5-12), and leads into the call to confess in 5:16.

p: James asks for mutual confession among believers. How it relates to confession to a priest is debated.
b: Exomologeisthe allelois means to admit openly to one another. The setting is the sickbed and the gathered church (5:14-15), and "to each other" is mutual. The Council of Trent read 5:14-15 as the sacrament of anointing, which "cleanses away sins, if there be any still to be expiated" (session 14, chapter 2). Calvin reports that his opponents cited 5:16 for confession to a priest, and answers that James "joins together mutual confession and mutual prayer" (Institutes 3.4.6). The Orthodox Confession of Dositheus grounds the mystery of penance in John 20:23, not in this verse (Decree 15). The deep dive on the chapter page gives the readings and their sources.

a: when it is put to work
p: Energoumene can mean "working" or "being made to work" by God.
b: The participle can be middle ("as it works") or passive ("when it is made effective", by God or the Spirit). The Plain English Translation keeps both open: the request of a righteous person "when it is put to work". "Righteous" here does not mean sinless: the example that follows is Elijah, "a man who felt what we feel".

p: A Hebrew way of adding force by repeating the verb.
b: The Greek proseuche proseuxato, "with prayer he prayed", copies a Hebrew pattern that doubles a verb to make it strong (as in Genesis 2:17, literally "dying you will die"). English does it with an adverb: "prayed earnestly". "A man who felt what we feel" renders homoiopathes, of the same feelings or nature: Elijah was no superman (compare his despair in 1 Kings 19:4).

p: 1 Kings says the rain came "in the third year". James and Luke say three years and six months.
b: Elijah told Ahab there would be "no dew and no rain unless I give the word" (1 Kings 17:1), and "in the third year" God sent him back (1 Kings 18:1). Jesus in Luke says "the sky was locked up for three years and six months" (Luke 4:25), the same figure as James. The longer count may come from Jewish tradition, or count from the start of the drought rather than from Elijah's stay in Zarephath. Three and a half years is also the length of trouble in Daniel ("a time, times and half a time", Daniel 7:25) and Revelation. 1 Kings never says Elijah prayed for the drought, but he prayed for its end, crouched with his face between his knees (1 Kings 18:42).
r: 1 Kings 17:1; 1 Kings 18:1; 1 Kings 18:41-45; Luke 4:25; Daniel 7:25; Revelation 11:6

p: Planao is to wander or be led astray, the word of 1:16. James ends where he began.
b: In 1:16 James warned, "Don't let yourselves be led astray." Now he closes the letter not with a greeting but with a task: bring back the one who has wandered. The word gives English "planet", a "wanderer" among the stars. Jesus told of the shepherd who goes after the one sheep that strays (Matthew 18:12-14, the same verb).

p: "His" can be the sinner who is brought back, or the one who brings him.
b: (1) Most read it of the sinner: turned back, he is saved from death at the judgment. (2) Some read it of the rescuer, as in Ezekiel's warning to the watchman: "you will have saved your own life" (Ezekiel 3:21). The same two readings apply to the sins covered. The Byzantine text has "will save a soul from death" (KJV); see the variant.

a: will lay a cover over a great number of sins
p: From Proverbs 10:12 in the Hebrew. 1 Peter 4:8 uses the same saying.
b: The Hebrew of Proverbs 10:12 reads, on this site: "Hatred rouses fights, but love lays a cover over all wrongdoing." The Greek translation of Proverbs says something different (love "covers all who do not love strife"), so James and 1 Peter 4:8 draw on the Hebrew, or on a saying already current among believers. 1 Peter 4:8 has "love lays a cover over a great number of sins", and James applies the saying to the work of bringing someone back. To "cover" sin is the Old Testament language of forgiveness (Psalm 32:1; Psalm 85:2).
